content:
If getting to your monitoring blood tests is hard, tell your GP practice or rheumatology team early rather than missing a test, because these tests check that your medicine is safe for you. Ask whether the test can be done closer to home (for example at your GP surgery rather than the hospital), at a time of day that suits your joints, or at home if you are housebound; what is available varies by area. If you have a medical or mobility need, you may qualify for free NHS non-emergency patient transport to hospital appointments, so ask your healthcare team or local patient transport service. In England, if you get certain benefits or have a low income, you may be able to claim back the cost of travel to hospital tests through the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme. If you do miss a test, call your team for advice; never stop a medicine yourself.

This guide is about the practical problem of getting to regular monitoring blood tests when arthritis, stiffness or other health problems make travel hard. To understand why the tests matter and what they check, see RA monitoring in later life and arthritis blood tests explained. If you take methotrexate, see methotrexate in later life.

Why it is worth solving, not skipping

Many medicines used for inflammatory arthritis need regular safety blood tests, for example to check your blood count, liver and kidneys. NICE says everyone with RA should have ongoing drug monitoring. Missing tests without telling anyone can mean your prescription is delayed or a problem is picked up late. The answer is to make the tests easier to get to, not to drop them.

Step 1: tell your team early

Ring your GP practice or rheumatology nurse before the next test is due and explain the problem plainly. For example: "I am struggling to get to the hospital for my blood tests because of my hips and I no longer drive. What are my options?" It helps to say:

  • how far you can walk and whether you can manage buses or steps
  • whether anyone can take you, and when
  • whether you have fallen recently or feel unsteady
  • if you are housebound, or caring for someone else

Step 2: ask where and when the test can be done

  • Closer to home. Many monitoring tests can be taken at a GP surgery or a local clinic rather than the hospital. Ask whether this is possible for yours
  • A better time of day. If morning stiffness makes early appointments hard, ask for a later slot
  • Combined visits. Ask whether the test can be done on the same day as another appointment
  • Booking. The NHS says some GP surgeries and hospitals let you book blood tests online
  • At home. If you are housebound, ask your GP practice whether a home visit for blood tests is possible. Arrangements differ between areas, so ask what your local service offers

NHS non-emergency patient transport

The NHS says some people can get free non-emergency patient transport to and from hospital, including people whose condition means they need extra support on the journey and people who find it difficult to walk. To find out if you are eligible and how to book, speak to your healthcare team or your local patient transport service.

In England, NHS England's eligibility criteria say most people are expected to travel independently or with help from family and friends, and that transport is for people who need it for their safety, safe mobility or condition. People likely to qualify include those with a significant mobility need, a medical need for support during the journey, or a cognitive or sensory impairment (such as dementia, or severe sight or hearing loss) that means they cannot travel safely another way. The appointment usually needs to be a hospital or specialist service you have been referred to, rather than a routine GP surgery visit.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run their own patient transport services with their own rules, so ask your clinic or health board.

Help with travel costs

In England, the NHS Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme can refund reasonable travel costs to hospital or other NHS premises for specialist tests or treatment if:

  • you or your partner get a qualifying benefit (such as Pension Credit Guarantee Credit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, or Universal Credit if you meet the criteria), or you qualify through the NHS Low Income Scheme
  • you have been referred for specialist NHS care or tests
  • the appointment is a separate visit from the one where you were referred

Refunds are normally based on the cheapest suitable way to travel for you, taking account of your age and medical condition. If you need a taxi, agree it with the hospital or your local integrated care board before you travel. You can also claim for an escort if a healthcare professional says it is medically necessary for someone to come with you. Claims are made at the hospital cashier's office with your receipts, appointment letter and proof of benefits, or by post on form HC5(T) within 3 months. Routine visits to a GP surgery are not covered. Other UK nations have their own schemes; ask your clinic.

Other ways to get there

  • Community transport schemes, often run by local charities, may offer door-to-door lifts. See community transport
  • A Blue Badge can make parking nearer the entrance possible. See Blue Badge with arthritis
  • Family, friends or neighbours may be glad to help if you ask for a specific day and time
  • Benefits: if travel and getting around are hard because of your arthritis, you may be eligible for disability benefits. See benefits and PIP

On the day

  • Wear loose sleeves you can roll up easily
  • Follow any instructions you were given about fasting or medicines before the test; if you were not given any, ask
  • Bring your appointment letter or form, a list of your medicines, and your glasses and hearing aids
  • Tell staff if you are worried about needles, find it hard to straighten your elbow, or need to sit or lie down. The NHS says you can bring someone with you for support
  • Allow time to rest before the journey home

Results can take a few days or longer. You may be able to see them in the NHS App. If you have heard nothing after a few weeks, contact the surgery or your specialist team.

If you miss a test

Call your GP practice or rheumatology advice line as soon as you can to rebook and ask what to do about your medicine in the meantime. Do not stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself; your team will tell you what is safe.

For family and carers

If you help someone to their tests, keep a simple calendar of when each test is due and who is taking them. Ask the team whether you can be the contact for appointments if the person agrees. If caring is becoming a lot, see carer's assessments.

When not to wait

  • Get urgent advice (your rheumatology advice line, GP or NHS 111) if you take a medicine that affects the immune system and get a high temperature, chills, a sore throat, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising or bleeding, or yellowing of the skin or eyes
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness, signs of a stroke, or if someone collapses
